_schema.what: One case in the case/1 shape (design/case/family-read.md §5), authored once as data and played with no model. Read by src/make/case.js (checkCase, fairPlay), src/make/talk.js (topicsFor, answer, truthCheck), src/make/narrator.js (checkNarrator, makeNarrator) and src/make/case-play.js (caseRequired, playCase; the panel lab/ui/talk-panel.js). Fields the contract sketch does not have are marked + here.
_schema.ids: Cast ids are bare (daniel); talk.js makes a topic person:<id> for asking about someone. In triples a person is person:<id>, a thing thing:<id>, a room room:<plan room id>, an event event:<id>; times are literals 'HH:MM' on the night of Friday 28 September 1660 (Julian) or the morning after. Room ids and opening ids are the plan's (src/make/plans/hybrid-e.js, built with GENTRY_SEAT_1660).
_schema.fact: + For a clue or claim, fact is the plain statement a voice may use (talk.js hands {id, text: fact} to the voice call and truthCheck holds it to them); triple is the same thing as a pattern-buffer assertion [subject, attribute, value] (the contract's fact:[s,a,v]).
_schema.hook: The no-model line. A person's clue: what they say when they tell it (talk.js says hook). A thing's clue: what you read when you look at the thing, open it or take it.
_schema.effect: genuine (a true cause of the ending) | false (a red herring held as a cause; names debunked_by) | context (texture; never fills a pillar alone). construct's coverage_effect.
_schema.tier: + essential (on a solution path, or a lie the path must break) | lead (points the way) | texture (colour and red herrings). Kept apart so the essentials are never buried (design/case/prior-art-interrogation.md §9).
_schema.gate: {topic, stance, requires:{learned:[clue ids], holding:[thing ids]}}: the clue is told when its topic is raised with one of its stances and every requirement is met. Stances: ask | press | show | accuse (chat never releases a clue). One gate per clue: case.js and talk.js read all-of requirements only.
_schema.claims: + What a person says on a topic where none of their clues is open: false:true is a lie, with why (the reason they tell it), press (the detail pressing gets, for when talk.js reads it), yield (what they say once it is broken: talk.js act refuse, and it stays broken) and broken_by (the clues or held things whose showing breaks it: talk.js answer(..., { stance: 'show', shown })). Anything else shown against a lie closes the person up for three turns with their guarded line. talk.js reads the first claim per topic, so each person has at most one claim a topic.
_schema.knows: + The person's own frame (knows:<id>): the true facts they hold, each {id, triple, text}. hides: which of them they keep back, why, and what brings them out. A voice may state only what a clue being told or a claim being said hands it.
_schema.voice: + {note (about 60 words), register, tics, phrases (6 to 8 period phrases, design/case/period-1660-death.md §4), address (how they name the others)}.
_schema.presence: Where a person can be found: [{room, when, doing}]; home is where they are at the start (narrator.js); when is 'start' or a narrator condition.
_schema.things: {id, kind (src/make/kinds), at (a plan room id, or another thing's id: in or on it), rel (+ in | on), slot (+ the host's slot), address (+ the birth address of a thing the house already builds), carry (false: fixed), key (+ the lock name a key opens), state (+ initial works.js states; ~burn is a process level), gate, clue (one id or a list), missing (+ what the house still lacks to build it)}.
_schema.clues: The clues things hold (construct's examine channel). People's clues live on each cast member.
_schema.doors: {openingId: {locked, key}}: the case's locks on the plan's openings, as reach.js reads them.
_schema.beats_clocks: narrator.js: when is its closed condition language (learned: holding: opened: said: at: here: var: genuine: misled: covered: fired: done: revealed: phase:, and counters); hook (40 words at most) is the no-model line; effects only spawn_person, move_person, set_var, reveal_thing.
_schema.accusation: + The no-model accusation in the panel's shape (lab/ui/talk-panel.js, case-play.js): one sentence of blanks, each {id, label, lead, options:[{id,label}]}, the suspect blank first; groups:[{id,label,keys}] confirmed a group at a time; truth:{key: option id}. supports: the learned clues that prove each true option (for the narrator's coverage and R59). attempts: wrong confirmations allowed before the verdict goes against you.
_schema._period: + Each period detail tagged S (sourced: the file and the source it cites) or C (chosen for the game).
_schema._house_needs: + What the house must still build for this case.
_schema._fairness: + The solution path, and the fair-play walk with what the checks measured.
_schema.label: + A short name on every clue, thing and claim, for the notebook, the evidence drawer and the truth check's lexicon (case-play.js label()).
_schema.cast_lines: + intro (what you see and hear when you first speak to them), deflect (a clue of theirs on the topic is still shut), dontknow (nothing in their frame), guarded (closed up after a wrong thing was shown).
_schema.what_happened: + The truth in plain words (who, motive, means, opportunity, the lock). Not named 'solution', because case-play.js reads k.solution before k.accusation.

title: The Evidence House
seed: Michaelmas morning, 1660. Mr Josias Hollins, steward of Wynstanton these thirty-one years, lies dead in the muniment room, its one door locked upon him and his key, they say, by his hand. At noon Sir Gervase Haywood is to seal the sale of his manor of Asshover to a London alderman.
theme: Faithful keeping against the hurry of money: the steward kept the house's evidences honest and was killed for it, and the truth must now be kept as carefully as he kept the deeds.

house.why_this_room: The muniment room has one door, from the closet off the best bedchamber; its two small windows are barred; the east wing's first floor (great chamber, withdrawing chamber, best bedchamber, closet, muniment room) is reached at night only by the great stair, whose foot passes the great parlour's door. The long gallery's west door is locked at nine (canon), so there is no back way.

when.inquest: Monday 1 October, in the great hall: the coroner from Chesterfield and a jury of the parish's householders summoned by the constable

player.role: a Justice of the Peace for the county, a neighbouring gentleman, sent for by Dame Anne at half past seven
player.can: examine anyone in the house and write down what they say; bind witnesses; commit a suspect to Derby gaol for the assizes

premise: You ride in at ten. Mr Hollins was found at a quarter past six, dead on the flags of the muniment room by the iron-bound chest, the door locked; his key, his clerk says, lay by his hand. Sir Gervase, abed with the gout, calls it a fall in a fit and means to seal at noon. The coroner sits on Monday.

victim.name: Mr Josias Hollins
victim.role: steward of Wynstanton since 1629, keeper of the evidences
victim.found: dead on the flags of the muniment room by the iron-bound chest, the door locked, at a quarter past six on Michaelmas morning
victim.now: laid out on his own bed in the steward's chamber for the coroner's view
victim.died: at about five past eleven on Michaelmas Eve, of a blow to the back of the head
victim.the_man: exact, honest, dry; kept the deeds through the wars and the sequestration; wore the door key at his girdle on a green cord; read every deed against its draft before it was sealed; never left a flame burning among the evidences

what_happened.motive: Bribed by Mr Cressy (twenty pieces of gold, as many again at the sealing), Daniel scraped the exception of the lead mines out of the second skin of the engrossment he had written, so the sale would pass the Asshover lead to Alderman Pargeter. Reading the engrossment against his own draft on Michaelmas Eve, Mr Hollins found the rasure in Daniel's hand and said he would take him and Mr Cressy before the justice in the morning.
what_happened.means: As the steward stooped at the north press for the Asshover deed, Daniel struck him on the back of the head with the brass candlestick from the table; the candle fell and went out. He laid the body by the iron-bound chest so that its corner would seem to have done it.
what_happened.opportunity: Daniel was in the muniment room with him from twenty to ten (Dame Anne came and went at ten) until after eleven. The only way down from the state rooms at night is the great stair, past the great parlour's open door: no one came down before twenty past eleven, when Mr Cressy saw Daniel; at half past, Francis saw him cross the screens passage.
what_happened.locked: To get out, Daniel cut the key from the steward's knotted girdle cord, locked the door from the closet side and kept the key. At dawn he was first to the door; when Ralph had opened it with Sir Gervase's key, Daniel went first into the dark room 'to open the shutters', let the key fall from his sleeve by the dead man's hand, and cried that he had found it. Dame Anne, holding the candle in the doorway, had seen the hand empty.
what_happened.in_one_line: The clerk who wrote the cheat killed the master who found it, locked the door with the key he cut from him, and brought the key back in at dawn.

timeline: 14 Sept

Mr Cressy and Mr Hollins agree the draft of the release of Asshover; the steward writes the exception of the mines in the margin and Cressy initials it 'agreed, A.C., 14 Sept.'; the steward pins a memorandum to the 1612 deed.
15 Sept
Cressy sends the agreed draft to Alderman Pargeter in London.
22 Sept
Pargeter's letter of the 18th reaches Cressy: the Asshover ore assays well; see the mines pass with the land.
Mon 24 Sept
Daniel begins engrossing the release on three skins from the steward's draft; skin 2 is written with the exception, and the steward looks it over.
Tue 25 Sept
In the stable yard Cressy gives Daniel twenty pieces of gold in a twist of paper with a note; Francis sees something pass.
Wed 26 Sept, night
Daniel scrapes the exception from skin 2, line 14, and writes 'together with all mines, minerals and quarries' over the rasure.
Fri 28 Sept, 18:00

Supper in the great chamber. Francis, in drink, tells the steward he'll not live to see the deed sealed. The steward says he will read the engrossment against the draft that night, as he does every deed before sealing. Cressy goes white; Dame Anne sees it.
Sir Gervase is carried to bed in the best bedchamber; at nine Dame Anne gives him his opiate.
The butler locks the long gallery's west door. Francis and Cressy sit down to tables in the great parlour with the door to the stair hall open for the fire.

The steward and Daniel pass the parlour door and go up the great stair with Daniel's chamber candle, the engrossment and the draft; through the great chamber, the withdrawing chamber, the best bedchamber (Sir Gervase asleep) and the closet. The steward closes the shutters, lights the table candle, and locks the door from within with the key on his girdle cord.

Dame Anne goes up the great stair (both card players see her) and knocks; the steward lets her in. She begs him to stay the sale until her new jointure is sealed. He has just found the rasure: his finger is on the line and his face is grey; Daniel, reading the draft aloud, falls silent. 'Not tonight, madam. There is something here I must see to first.'
Dame Anne comes down (seen) and goes back to the nursery by the back stair. The steward locks the door after her and reads on to the end in silence.

The steward holds skin 2 to the candle: 'This is thy hand, Daniel. Who paid thee?' He says Daniel and Mr Cressy shall go before the justice in the morning, and turns to the north press for the 1612 deed.

As he stoops at the drawer 'Asshover / Feoffments i', Daniel strikes him on the back of the head with the brass candlestick from the table. The candle falls and goes out on the flags; Daniel's chamber candle, on the chest lid, still burns.

Daniel drags the body to the iron-bound chest and lays the head by its corner; puts the table candle back crooked in its stick and the stick on the table; takes the draft; cuts the key from the knotted girdle cord with his penknife; unlocks the door, goes out, locks it again from the closet side, and keeps the key.
Francis goes to the buttery to draw canary; Cressy sits alone at the parlour table.
Daniel comes down the great stair, his candle shielded; Cressy sees him through the open door, and Daniel sees Cressy see him.
Daniel crosses the screens passage from the hall door to the kitchen passage; Francis, at the buttery door with a jug and a cut hand, sees him.

Daniel reaches the west garret by the kitchen, the larder and the back stair, and hides the draft in his chest with the gold and the note. Francis comes back to the parlour bleeding; Cressy binds the hand with his own handkerchief, marked A.C.

Francis and Cressy go to bed by the back stair, through the steward's chamber (his bed unslept), the cook's chamber and the west closet. Dame Anne, at the nursery door, sees Francis on the landing with blood on his hand and shirt.
Margery the cook finds the steward's bed unslept and tells Daniel at the back stair.
Daniel is first to the muniment door, knocking and calling. Ralph takes Sir Gervase's key from the nail at the bed-head (Sir Gervase sleeps on); Dame Anne comes with a candle.

Ralph unlocks the door: it was locked fast. The room is dark. Daniel goes in first 'to open the shutters'; Dame Anne, holding the candle in the doorway, sees the dead man's hand on the flags, open and empty. Daniel kneels by him, lets the key fall from his sleeve, cries that it lay by his master's hand, takes it up and lays it on the table, and opens the shutters.
Sir Gervase, woken and in pain, calls it a fall in a fit: send to the coroner and to a justice, and seal at noon regardless.

The body is carried to the steward's chamber; Dame Anne and Margery wash it and lay it out. She sees the wound at the back of the head and the cut cord at the girdle. A maid scrubs the flags by the chest.
Cressy takes the engrossment from the muniment table to the draw-table in the great chamber.
Dame Anne sends a groom for the justice, four miles off; the constable goes to the coroner at Chesterfield.
The justice arrives (the player). Daniel keeps the muniment door; Cressy keeps the engrossment; Francis nurses his hand in the great parlour; Dame Anne meets the justice in the hall.

cast.intro: (A thin young man in black, ink on his fingers, standing at the muniment door as if it might be taken from him.) Your Worship. Daniel Wragg, Mr Hollins's clerk. I have kept the door since we found him. Nothing has been moved, sir, but the engrossment Mr Cressy carried off.

voice.note: Twenty-two, the Wynstanton schoolmaster's son, taught a fair engrossing hand by Mr Hollins and grieving him truly. Speaks low and exact, with a copyist's care for hours and words; quotes his master; Bible cadences from his mother. When he lies he grows more precise, not less, and rubs the ink on his second finger. Never coarse, never sly.

claims.line: We read the engrossment against the draft till half past ten, your Worship. I heard the hall clock go the half as I came down the stair. My master bid me to bed; he said he would sit a while alone, and I heard him turn the key behind me.
claims.press: Half past ten, sir. I'm a clerk; I mark the hours. Down the great stair, through the hall and the kitchen, and up the back stair to my bed.
claims.yield: (He is quiet a long moment.) Then I was out in the hour, your Worship. It was later. I was afraid to say how late, for how it would look.
claims.why: puts him out of the room more than half an hour before the blow

claims.yield: (He looks at the key, and then at his hands.) I found it by him, sir. I... I'll say no more about the key.

cast.deflect: I couldn't say, your Worship. I'd not like to say what I don't know.
cast.dontknow: I know nothing of that, sir.
cast.guarded: (He folds his inky hands.) I've told your Worship all I know.

cast.name: Mr Ambrose Cressy
cast.role: attorney of Clifford's Inn, agent for Alderman Pargeter, the buyer
cast.intro: (A spare man in good black and a lawyer's bands, standing over a table laid with parchment, wax and bags of money.) Ambrose Cressy, sir, of Clifford's Inn, for Alderman Pargeter. A sad business. I trust it need not keep us past noon.

presence.doing: by the draw-table, the engrossment and the purchase money before him
booted, his cloak over his arm, waiting for his horse
with the household before Sir Gervase

cast.night: At tables with Francis in the great parlour from nine until near one; alone at the table from a quarter past eleven, while Francis was at the buttery, and saw Daniel come down the great stair at about twenty past; bound Francis's hand; to bed at one in the west bedchamber.

voice.note: Forty-five, an attorney of Clifford's Inn, agent for Alderman Pargeter of London. Courteous London speech with a lawyer's hedges; turns every question into terms, dates and sums, and counts on his fingers. Dislikes the country, its mud and its hours. Calm while he holds the papers; when his own hand is shown him he bargains, plainly and quickly, and never pleads.
voice.register: a London professional man's courtesy, formal and dry
phrases: I'll not trouble you with the particulars

triple: the exception of the mines, 14 September
knows.text: He agreed the exception of the mines with the steward on 14 September and initialled it.

triple: 'See the mines pass with the land', 18 September
knows.text: Alderman Pargeter wrote that the ore assays well and the mines must pass with the land.

triple: person:daniel twenty pieces of gold, Tuesday 25 September
knows.text: He gave Daniel twenty pieces of gold in the stable yard on Tuesday, with a note promising as many at the sealing, to leave the exception out of the second skin.
At supper the steward said he would read the engrossment against the draft that night.

triple: person:daniel come down the great stair, 23:20
knows.text: At about twenty past eleven, alone at the table, he saw the clerk come down the great stair, his candle shielded, white in the face.
Francis went down for wine at a quarter past eleven and came back with his hand cut; Cressy bound it with his handkerchief.
He took the engrossment from the muniment table this morning.
He holds Francis's note of hand for sixty pounds lost at tables.
Dame Anne went up a little before ten and came down within the quarter hour.
He never left the parlour from nine until one.

hides.why: the cheat would cost him his practice and his principal
hides.until: shown the gold and the note (cressy_bribe), or the steward's memorandum with his own agreement and his principal's letter (cressy_cheat)

hides.why: the clerk, accused, would name him for the bribe
hides.until: his own cheat is out (the gold note learned)

claims.label: Mr Cressy: who is in the house
claims.fact: Dame Anne has the house in hand; the heir is in the parlour; the clerk keeps the muniment door.
claims.line: Dame Anne has the house in hand, sir. The heir is in the parlour with his beer, the clerk sits on the muniment door like a hen on eggs, and I wait on a seal.

claims.label: Cressy: the mines never excepted
claims.fact: Mr Cressy says the mines were never excepted in the agreed draft.
claims.line: The mines were never excepted, sir. The draft as agreed says nothing of them; you may see my own copy, as it came from London.
claims.press: As to that, I am instructed the land passes entire, with its appurtenances. If the steward fancied otherwise, he never said so to me.
claims.yield: My initials. Yes. I agreed it on the fourteenth to have peace, and my principal would not have it. You may guess the rest; I'll not say it for you.
claims.why: hides that he agreed the exception and then had it cut out

claims.label: Cressy: saw the clerk only going up
claims.fact: Mr Cressy says he saw the clerk go up with the steward at twenty to ten, and not again.
claims.line: The clerk? A careful young man. I saw him go up with the steward at twenty to ten, and not again.
claims.press: I attend to my cards, sir, not to the stair.
claims.yield: (He sets down his pen.) I saw him. I'll tell you what I saw when you tell me what you have.
claims.why: the clerk, accused, would name him for the bribe

claims.label: Cressy: a clerk's correction
claims.fact: Mr Cressy says the scrape on the second skin is a clerk's correction that does not touch the sense.
claims.line: A clerk's correction on the second skin, sir. They are common enough, and it does not touch the sense.
claims.press: With submission, a rasure in an unsealed engrossment is nothing; it may be written fair again before noon.
claims.yield: It touches the sense. I'll not pretend it doesn't.

claims.label: Cressy: knows nothing of the clerk's money
claims.fact: Mr Cressy says he knows nothing of the clerk's money.
claims.line: I know nothing of the clerk's money, sir.
claims.press: Servants are paid, and vails are given. I have given a shilling to every groom in this house.

claims.label: Cressy: at tables till one
claims.fact: Mr Cressy sat at tables in the great parlour from nine until one.
claims.line: At tables, sir, with Mr Haywood, from nine until near one. I never left the room.

claims.label: Cressy: the bond and the sale
claims.fact: Alderman Pargeter lent Sir Gervase two thousand pounds on bond in 1655; he takes Asshover at a fair price, less the bond.
claims.line: My principal lent Sir Gervase two thousand pounds on bond in 'fifty-five, sir. The day is long past. He takes Asshover at a fair price, less the bond, and Sir Gervase is out of debt. Everyone is served.

claims.label: Cressy: Francis plays deep
claims.fact: Francis plays deep and loses handsomely.
claims.line: A young gentleman who plays deep and loses handsomely, sir. I bear him no ill will.

claims.label: Cressy: sixty pounds and a note of hand
claims.fact: Francis lost sixty pounds at tables and gave Mr Cressy his note of hand.
claims.line: We played for money, sir; gentlemen do. Mr Haywood lost sixty pounds and gave me his note for it. I'd thank you not to make a noise of it before his father.

clues.label: Cressy: at tables till one
clues.fact: Mr Cressy says he sat at tables with Francis in the great parlour from nine until near one and never left the room.
clues.hook: I sat at tables with Mr Haywood in the great parlour from nine until near one, sir, and never stirred from the room. He'll tell you so, and what it cost him, if he's honest.

clues.label: Cressy: Dame Anne up and down by a quarter past ten
clues.fact: Mr Cressy saw Dame Anne go up the great stair a little before ten and come down within the quarter hour.
clues.hook: Dame Anne went up the great stair a little before ten and came down within the quarter hour. We had the door open for the fire's draw; one sees the stair foot from the table.

clues.label: Cressy: Francis cut his hand in the buttery
triple: on a glass in room:buttery, 23:15 to 23:35
clues.fact: Mr Cressy says Francis went down for wine at a quarter past eleven and came back with his hand cut on a glass, and he bound it with his own handkerchief.
clues.hook: He went down for more wine at a quarter past eleven and came back bleeding like a Martinmas hog, sir. A glass broke in his hand. I bound it with my own handkerchief; you'll find my mark on it.

clues.label: Cressy took the engrossment
clues.fact: Mr Cressy took the engrossment from the muniment table this morning, before the justice came.
clues.hook: I took it up from the muniment table this morning, sir, when they carried him out. It is my principal's deed, to be sealed at noon, and I'd not leave it in a dead man's room for any hand to come at.

clues.label: Cressy paid Daniel to leave out the mines
triple: person:daniel twenty pieces of gold to leave the exception of the mines out of skin 2
clues.fact: Mr Cressy owns he paid Daniel twenty pieces of gold, and promised as many at the sealing, to engross the second skin without the exception of the mines.
clues.hook: Very well. I gave the boy twenty pieces to leave the mines out of the second skin, and promised as many at the sealing. That is a cheat, sir, and a matter for Chancery. It is not murder. I never set foot on that stair.

clues.label: Cressy owns the mines were cut from the engrossment
triple: the exception of the mines from skin 2, by the clerk who engrossed it
clues.fact: Mr Cressy owns that Alderman Pargeter wanted the mines, that he agreed the exception on the 14th only to have peace, and that he had the clerk who engrossed the deed leave it out of the second skin.
clues.hook: You have read my letters, then. Very well: my principal would have the mines, and I agreed the exception on the fourteenth only to have peace. I had the clerk who engrossed it leave it out of the second skin. A cheat, sir, and a matter for Chancery. It is not murder.

clues.label: Cressy saw Daniel come down at twenty past eleven
triple: person:daniel come down the great stair alone, 23:20
clues.fact: Mr Cressy saw Daniel come down the great stair alone at about twenty past eleven, while Francis was at the buttery, his candle shielded and his face white.
clues.hook: Since we are plain now: at twenty past eleven, while Mr Haywood was at the buttery, the clerk came down the great stair alone. He kept his candle behind his hand and he was white as his bands. He saw me see him.

cast.deflect: As to that, sir, I should want to see what you are driving at.
cast.dontknow: I know nothing of it, sir. I am a stranger in this house.
cast.guarded: With submission, sir, I'll answer questions, not riddles.

cast.name: Mr Francis Haywood
cast.intro: (A young man by the parlour fire, his right hand bound in a fine handkerchief, a pot of small beer at his elbow.) Francis Haywood. You'll be the justice. Sit, if you like; my father's chairs are still ours till noon.

presence.doing: by the parlour fire with small beer and a bound hand
with the household before Sir Gervase

cast.night: At tables with Cressy in the great parlour from nine, the door to the stair hall open; to the buttery for canary at about a quarter past eleven, where he broke a glass and cut his hand; coming out at about half past, saw Daniel cross the screens passage; back by twenty-five to twelve; to bed at one by the back stair.

voice.note: Twenty-six, Sir Gervase's heir, grown up in the sequestration years and sour with it. Quick, proud and sardonic; answers a question with a question; mild oaths. Calls Cressy 'the alderman's man' and his stepmother 'madam'. Grieves the steward more than he shows. Drinks small beer this morning for his head. Lies badly and not for long; generous once he stops defending himself.
voice.register: a young Cavalier gentleman's easy, edged speech
tics: bitter jokes about his father's loyalty
phrases: what would you have of me?

knows.text: He sat at tables with Cressy in the great parlour from nine until one, the door open.

triple: £60 to person:cressy, on his note of hand
knows.text: He lost sixty pounds to Cressy and gave his note of hand.

triple: person:hollins and person:daniel go up the great stair, 21:40
knows.text: He saw the steward and Daniel go up at twenty to ten.

triple: person:anne go up 21:50 and come down 22:10
knows.text: He saw his stepmother go up a little before ten and come down at ten past.

triple: come down the great stair, 22:10 to 23:15
knows.text: No one else came down the great stair while he sat at the table.
The gallery's west door is locked at nine; there's no other way down from the state rooms at night.

triple: on a glass at the canary hogshead, 23:15 to 23:35
knows.text: He drew canary in the buttery past eleven, broke the glass and cut his hand.

triple: person:daniel cross the screens passage alone, 23:25
knows.text: Coming out of the buttery near half past eleven he saw Daniel cross the screens passage from the hall door to the kitchen passage, alone, his candle shaking.
Cressy bound his hand with his own handkerchief.

triple: person:cressy give person:daniel something heavy in paper, stable yard, Tuesday 25 September
knows.text: On Tuesday in the stable yard he saw Cressy put something heavy in a twist of paper into Daniel's hand.
The steward's bed was empty when he went through to his own at one.

triple: the steward would not live to see the deed sealed
knows.text: At supper, in drink, he said the steward would not live to see the deed sealed.
His father has excepted the mines of Asshover in every grant since his grandfather bought it.

hides.why: his father would stop his allowance for the play and the debt, and he'll not have it said he was drunk in the buttery the night the steward died
hides.until: pressed about his cut hand once Dame Anne's word of it is known (anne_francis_blood), or shown the broken glass

hides.why: to tell it he must own where he was
hides.until: the same: once he owns the buttery he tells what he saw from its door

claims.label: Francis: who is in the house
claims.fact: Dame Anne runs the house; Cressy is upstairs in the great chamber with the purchase money; the clerk keeps the muniment door.
claims.line: My stepmother runs the house, as you see. Cressy is upstairs in the great chamber, counting my inheritance into bags, and the clerk keeps the muniment door as if the old man might get up and walk.

claims.label: Francis: abed by eleven
claims.fact: Francis says he was abed by eleven.
claims.line: I was abed by eleven, sir, and slept like the dead. Ask the alderman's man; he'll tell you we went up together.
claims.press: Abed, I said. Would you have me swear it?
claims.yield: Very well: not abed. I was in the buttery past eleven. Ask me of my hand, and I'll tell you the whole of it.
claims.why: hides the deep play, the debt and the drinking

claims.label: Francis: cut at supper
claims.fact: Francis says he cut his hand on a glass at supper.
claims.line: I cut it on a glass at supper. Clumsy.
claims.press: At supper, sir. Ask anyone who sat there.
claims.yield: Not at supper. In the buttery, past eleven, drawing canary like a footman. There: you have my shame.
claims.why: the same: the night he will not own

claims.label: Francis: played for love
claims.fact: Francis says they played for love.
claims.line: We played for love, sir, to pass the evening.
claims.press: For love. A few shillings, perhaps.
claims.yield: For money. Sixty pounds I haven't got, and the alderman's man has my note for it. Don't tell my father until I do.

claims.label: Francis: the sale
claims.fact: Sir Gervase sells Asshover to pay the debts of the wars.
claims.line: My father sells Asshover to pay for his loyalty, sir. The King came home; our money did not. The alderman lent on bond five years since, and now he takes the best of our land for it.

claims.label: Francis: Daniel, Hollins's shadow
claims.fact: Daniel was the steward's shadow, a good clerk.
claims.line: Daniel? Hollins's shadow. A good clerk and a better copyist. He'd not say boo to a goose.

claims.label: Francis: ask her
claims.fact: Dame Anne went up to the muniment room at ten.
claims.line: I've told you: ask her what she wanted in the muniment room at ten at night.

claims.label: Francis: his letters
claims.fact: Mr Hollins taught Francis his letters while Sir Gervase was at the wars.
claims.line: He taught me my letters, sir, when my father was at the wars.

clues.label: Francis: no one came down at half past ten
triple: come down the great stair, 22:10 to 23:15
clues.fact: Francis says no one came down the great stair at half past ten: the parlour door stood open and they would have seen a light; Dame Anne came down at ten past ten and no one after her while he sat there; and the gallery is locked at nine, so there is no other way down.
clues.hook: Half past ten? He never came down at half past ten. The parlour door stood open for the fire, and you can't come off that stair without your light passing it. My stepmother came down at ten past ten. Nobody after her while I sat there, and there's no other way down at night: the gallery's locked at nine.

clues.label: Francis saw Daniel in the screens passage at half past eleven
triple: person:daniel cross the screens passage alone, 23:25
clues.fact: Francis owns he went to the buttery for canary at a quarter past eleven and cut his hand on a glass; coming out near half past, he saw Daniel cross the screens passage from the hall door to the kitchen passage, alone, his candle shaking.
clues.hook: Pox on it: yes, since my stepmother has told you. I went to the buttery for canary at a quarter past eleven and broke the glass in my hand; look at the hogshead if you doubt me. Coming out, near half past, I saw Daniel cross the passage from the hall door to the kitchen passage. Alone. His candle shook like a leaf.

clues.label: Francis: Cressy never left the table
clues.fact: Francis says Cressy never left the table before he himself went down for wine past eleven.
clues.hook: Cressy on the stair at half past ten? He never stirred from that table but to deal, till I went down for wine past eleven. Whoever told you so is a liar.

clues.label: Francis: Dame Anne went up at ten
clues.fact: Francis says his stepmother went up to the muniment room a little before ten.
clues.hook: Ask my stepmother why she went up to the muniment room at ten o'clock at night. She'll tell you she was in the nursery.

clues.label: Francis saw Cressy pass Daniel something heavy
triple: person:cressy give person:daniel something heavy in paper, Tuesday 25 September
clues.fact: Francis saw Cressy put something heavy in a twist of paper into Daniel's hand in the stable yard on Tuesday, and Daniel hid it in his doublet.
clues.hook: The lead? My father has kept the mines out of every grant of Asshover since my grandfather bought it. Has the alderman's man been at them? Then hear this: on Tuesday in the stable yard I saw him put something in Daniel's hand, heavy, in a twist of paper, and the boy hid it in his doublet like a thief. I took it for a vail.

clues.label: Francis's words at supper
triple: the steward would not live to see the deed sealed
clues.fact: Francis owns he said at supper the steward would not live to see the deed sealed, meaning the sale would break his heart.
clues.hook: I said at supper he'd not live to see it sealed. God forgive me. I meant the sale would break his heart. He kept this house through the wars, sir, when my father was in the field and the committee men were at the door.

clues.label: The steward's bed empty at one
clues.fact: Francis says the steward's bed was empty when he and Cressy went through his chamber to bed at one.
clues.hook: I know nothing of how he died, sir. I know his bed was empty when Cressy and I went through his chamber to ours at one. I thought him still at his deeds.

cast.deflect: Ask me something I can answer, sir.
cast.dontknow: How should I know? Ask the clerk; he knows everything in this house.
cast.guarded: Pox on it, sir, I've done with your questions for a while.

cast.name: Dame Anne Haywood
cast.role: Sir Gervase's second wife, mistress of the household
cast.intro: (A composed woman in dark silk, her keys at her waist, who has not slept.) Your Worship. I am Anne Haywood; I sent for you, since Sir Gervase cannot leave his bed. I'll answer what I can.

presence.doing: sitting by the door of Sir Gervase's chamber
with the household before Sir Gervase

cast.night: Gave Sir Gervase his opiate at nine; went up to the muniment room from ten to ten until ten past ten to beg the steward to stay the sale; back to the nursery by the back stair; at one saw Francis on the back stair landing with blood on his hand; at dawn held the candle at the muniment door; at seven washed and laid out the body with Margery.

voice.note: Thirty-eight, Sir Gervase's second wife, Ned's mother, the mistress of the household. Composed and exact; answers in household facts: candles, linen, the hour the bread came in. Prayer-book turns of phrase and a quiet irony. Turns her wedding ring when she hides something. Fears for her son's portion more than for herself. Once her own secret is out, she is the plainest witness in the house.
voice.register: a gentlewoman's composed courtesy, plain and exact
tics: turns her wedding ring when hiding
phrases: as the Prayer Book has it

knows.text: She gave Sir Gervase his opiate at nine; he heard nothing after.
She went up a little before ten to beg the steward to stay the sale until her new jointure was sealed.

triple: a line of the engrossment, grey-faced, 21:50
knows.text: She found him grey-faced over the engrossment with his finger on a line; Daniel, reading the draft aloud, stopped when she came in; Mr Hollins said, 'Not tonight, madam. There is something here I must see to first.'
He locked the door behind her.
Her jointure of £250 a year is charged on Asshover; she must join in a fine to let it go and is promised a new one on Tibshelfe.

triple: on the back stair at 01:00 with blood on his hand
knows.text: Francis came up the back stair after one, singing, with blood on his hand and his shirt.

triple: the steward would not live to see the deed sealed
knows.text: At supper Francis swore the steward would not live to see the deed sealed.

triple: at supper, when the collation was named
knows.text: Mr Cressy went white at supper when Mr Hollins said he would read the engrossment against the draft that night.

triple: the hand of person:hollins empty before person:daniel knelt, 06:15
knows.text: At dawn she held the candle in the doorway; Daniel went in first, to the shutters he said; she saw the dead man's hand on the flags, open and empty, before Daniel knelt by it and cried that the key lay there.

triple: at the back of the head, round, the size of a crown piece
knows.text: She washed the body: the wound is at the back of the head, round, the size of a crown piece; the chest's corner is square.
When they laid him out his key-cord hung cut from his girdle.

triple: on a nail at his bed-head
knows.text: Sir Gervase's key hangs on a nail at his bed-head; Ralph took it down at dawn to open the door.
Sir Gervase has excepted the mines of Asshover in every lease and grant since his father bought it.

hides.why: she went behind her husband's back to stay his sale, and a lady alone with the steward at night is talk
hides.until: she learns she was seen on the stair (francis_names_anne) and is pressed

hides.why: her fear for her son is not the household's business

claims.label: Dame Anne: who is in the house
claims.fact: Daniel Wragg keeps the muniment door, in the closet off the best bedchamber; Mr Cressy is in the great chamber with the engrossment and the purchase money; Francis is by the great parlour fire; Sir Gervase keeps his bed.
claims.line: (She counts them off.) Daniel Wragg, the clerk, keeps the muniment door, in the closet off the best bedchamber, up the great stair. Mr Cressy, the buyer’s attorney, sits in the great chamber with the engrossment and the money. My husband’s son Francis is by the great parlour fire. Sir Gervase keeps his bed; I beg you will not trouble him. The servants are below, if your Worship wants them.

claims.label: Dame Anne: in the nursery all evening
claims.fact: Dame Anne says she was in the nursery with Ned all the evening and abed by ten.
claims.line: I was in the nursery with Ned all the evening, your Worship, and abed by ten.
claims.press: In the nursery. Ned had the toothache; his nurse will tell you.
claims.yield: (She turns her ring.) Very well: not the nursery. Where I was is my own affair, and Sir Gervase's. Ask Francis what he saw, since he watches me so close.
claims.why: hides her visit to the steward, against her husband's sale

claims.label: Dame Anne: the door at dawn
triple: door d21 with Sir Gervase's key, 06:15
claims.fact: Ralph opened the door with Sir Gervase's key; it was locked fast; Daniel went in first; she held the light.
claims.line: Ralph opened it with Sir Gervase's key, your Worship; it was locked fast. Daniel went in first, to the shutters, and I held the light in the door. He lay by the chest. God rest him.

claims.label: Dame Anne: the sale
claims.fact: Sir Gervase must sell; the composition and the war debts have eaten them; Asshover goes to the alderman who lent on bond.
claims.line: Sir Gervase must sell, your Worship. The composition and the war debts have eaten us. Asshover goes to the alderman who lent on bond five years since.

claims.label: Dame Anne: Daniel at the door
claims.fact: Daniel has not left the muniment door all morning.
claims.line: Daniel loved him like a father, I think. He has not left that door all morning.

claims.label: Dame Anne: the wound
triple: at the back of the head
claims.fact: The wound is at the back of his head, and round.
claims.line: As I told your Worship: at the back of the head, and round, as if something round had struck him.

claims.label: Dame Anne: the steward in the wars
claims.fact: Mr Hollins kept the evidences through the wars and hid them from the committee men.
claims.line: He kept our evidences through the wars, your Worship. When the committee men came in 'forty-five he had the deeds in the malt-kiln before they were through the gate.

clues.label: The wound: behind, and round
triple: at the back of the head, round; the chest's corner is square
clues.fact: Dame Anne washed the body: the wound is at the back of the head, round, the size of a crown piece, while the chest's corner he is said to have fallen on is square.
clues.hook: I washed him myself, with Margery. The wound was at the back of his head, round, the size of a crown piece. Sir Gervase will have it he fell forward on the chest. The chest's corner is square, your Worship, and he was struck behind.

clues.label: The key-cord cut at his girdle
clues.fact: When they laid him out, the green cord of his key hung cut from his girdle.
clues.hook: When we laid him out, his key-cord hung from his girdle, cut. I thought the men had cut it lifting him. Now I think on it, none of them had a knife out.

clues.label: Sir Gervase's key on its nail
triple: on a nail at his bed-head
clues.fact: Sir Gervase's key hangs on a nail at his bed-head; he slept on his opiate from nine; Ralph took the key down at dawn to open the door.
clues.hook: Sir Gervase's key hangs on a nail at his bed-head. He took his opiate at nine and heard nothing after, God help him; anyone who passed his bed might have reached it. Ralph took it down at dawn to open the door.

clues.label: Dame Anne: his hand was empty at dawn
triple: the hand of person:hollins empty before person:daniel knelt, 06:15
clues.fact: At dawn Dame Anne held the candle in the doorway; Daniel went in first, to the shutters he said; she saw the dead man's hand on the flags, open and empty, before Daniel knelt by it; then he cried that the key lay by his hand.
clues.hook: I held the candle in the doorway this morning. Daniel went in before me, to open the shutters, he said. I saw Mr Hollins's hand on the flags in my light, open, and nothing in it or by it. Then Daniel knelt, and cried out that the key lay by his hand.

clues.label: Dame Anne: Francis bloody on the stair at one
triple: on the back stair at 01:00 with blood on his hand
clues.fact: Dame Anne saw Francis come up the back stair after one with blood on his hand and shirt; at supper he had said the steward would not live to see the deed sealed.
clues.hook: Francis came up the back stair after one, singing, with blood on his hand and his shirt. At supper he swore Mr Hollins would not live to see the deed sealed. I tell you because you'll hear it from the servants.

clues.label: Dame Anne's visit at ten
triple: a line of the engrossment, grey-faced, 21:50
clues.fact: Dame Anne owns she went up at ten to beg the steward to stay the sale; he was grey-faced over the engrossment with his finger on a line, Daniel stopped reading the draft when she came in, and Mr Hollins said, 'Not tonight, madam. There is something here I must see to first.' She came down; he locked the door behind her; he was alive.
clues.hook: Yes. I went up a little before ten, to beg him to stay the sale until my new jointure was sealed. He had the engrossment under the candle and his finger on one line, and his face was grey. Daniel was reading the draft aloud, and stopped when I came in. Mr Hollins said, 'Not tonight, madam. There is something here I must see to first.' I came down. He locked the door behind me. He was alive.

clues.label: The mines always excepted
clues.fact: Sir Gervase has excepted the mines of Asshover in every lease and grant since his father bought it; Mr Hollins saw to it.
clues.hook: Sir Gervase has excepted the mines of Asshover in every lease and grant since his father bought it. Mr Hollins saw to it. He used to say the lead was the one thing the war had not taken from us.

clues.label: Cressy went white at supper
triple: at supper, when the collation was named

_period.what: An inquest within about 48 hours, by the coroner with a jury of 12 to 24 householders summoned by the parish constable, often held where the death happened; the jury views the body.

_period.what: The inquest on Monday 1 October in the great hall, the coroner from Chesterfield; the body kept laid out on the steward's own bed for the view.
Verdicts: felo de se forfeits the dead man's goods; accident and natural death do not. Sir Gervase wants 'a fall in a fit' so nothing delays the sale.
'By the visitation of God' as the jury's phrase for a natural death.
_period.note: the research found no source for it (gap)

_period.what: The player as a Justice of the Peace, a neighbouring gentleman who takes statements, binds witnesses and commits to gaol for the assizes; Derby gaol, the next assizes.
_period.note: the JP's manual (Dalton, The Country Justice, a 1666 edition) is S; its procedure for examinations was not read (gap)

_period.what: Michaelmas Day, 29 September 1660, fell on a Saturday (Julian calendar), so Michaelmas Eve was a Friday and the inquest waits for Monday; Cressy's bribe on Tuesday the 25th.

Optional: the padlock key in the table's drawer and Sir Gervase's in the closet's cabinet open the chest -> jointure_settlement.
5. The withdrawing chamber: press Dame Anne on This morning, or show her the key -> anne_dawn (locked). Beats lie_key, then garret_flight: Daniel runs to the west garret.

6. Down the great stair to the great parlour. Francis: about Daniel -> francis_no_one_down (opportunity), beat lie_half_ten; The lead -> francis_saw_purse (lead); about Cressy -> francis_cressy_sat (breaks Daniel's herring); about Dame Anne -> francis_names_anne (a red herring); press him on his cut hand -> francis_saw_daniel (opportunity).

7. The west garret, by the hall, the screens passage, the kitchen, the larder and the back stair. Daniel at his chest (beat cornered). Open the chest and the oak box -> gold_note (motive); take the steward's draft -> draft_exception (motive). Show Daniel the gold: his lie about it breaks.

8. Leaving the garret the household gathers in the great hall (beat gather). Show Cressy the gold -> cressy_bribe (motive), and about Daniel -> cressy_saw_daniel (opportunity); show him the draft on The lead: his lie breaks.

9. Accuse: Daniel Wragg killed Mr Hollins because the steward found the cheat in the engrossment, written for gold; he died of a blow from behind with the table candlestick; the murderer was with him by staying on in the muniment room past eleven; the door was locked with his own key, cut from his girdle and dropped by his hand at dawn.
other_routes: Motive without Daniel's chest: the open drawer (drawer_asshover) breaks Cressy's lie about the mines; his own papers in the chest at his bed's foot (pargeter_letter) then make him own the cheat (cressy_cheat).
Opportunity without Daniel's words: press Francis on his cut hand once Dame Anne has told of it (francis_saw_daniel), or show Cressy the gold (cressy_saw_daniel).
Means without the candlestick: Dame Anne's account of the wound (anne_wound) or the clean chest band (chest_band_clean).
With the engrossment kind built, its rasure proves the motive from the great chamber's draw-table.

_fairness.keys_and_doors: No door is locked in play: d21, the muniment room's one door, was opened at dawn with Sir Gervase's key and left unlocked (doors.d21). The only locks are the chest's two padlocks; their keys lie in the muniment table's drawer and in the closet's japanned cabinet, outside the chest, and nothing essential is in it.

red_herrings.points_at: Daniel says he left Mr Hollins alive at half past ten, heard him lock the door behind him, and went down the great stair to bed.
Daniel says the key lay on the flags by his master's hand when the door was opened, so his master had locked himself in.
Daniel says that as he came down at half past ten he passed Mr Cressy going up the great stair, who said he sought the close stool in the closet.
Francis says his stepmother went up to the muniment room a little before ten.
Dame Anne saw Francis come up the back stair after one with blood on his hand and shirt; at supper he had said the steward would not live to see the deed sealed.
Mr Cressy's copy of the draft, as it came from London, passes Asshover with its appurtenances and says nothing of the mines.
Sir Gervase's key hangs on a nail at his bed-head; he slept on his opiate from nine; Ralph took the key down at dawn to open the door.

notes: fairPlay is generous by design: it assumes every topic and stance gets tried. The scripted play is the honest order, through talk.js as a player meets it.
Circumstantial clues are leads, not genuine (francis_saw_purse, anne_girdle_cord, body_cord), so the narrator's phases follow real proof: the pressure phase arrives with the garret, not before.
case.js and talk.js read one all-of gate per clue. Dame Anne's visit (anne_visit) asks for Francis's word only, though Cressy's or Daniel's would serve as well; her yield sends you to Francis.
The gather beat waits while you are with Daniel, so you can confront him at his chest; saddled cannot follow gather.

parts.text: A deed of parchment, its seal on a tag, under the Letters Patent and the Pardon.
This Indenture

made the sixth day of May in the yeare of our Lord God one thousand six hundred and fiftie, Betweene Sir Gervase Haywood of Wynstanton in the County of Derby, Baronet, of the one part, and his Trustees &c. of the other part.

Witnesseth that in consideration of a marriage shortly to be had and solemnized betweene the said Sir Gervase and Anne his intended wife, and for a competent jointure for her, the said Sir Gervase hath granted unto the said Trustees one annuity or yearely rent charge of Two hundred and fiftie pounds of lawfull money of England, to be issuing out of the Mannor of Asshover in the said County and all the lands thereunto belonging, To the use of the said Anne for the terme of her naturall life for her jointure, payable at the Feasts of the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin Mary and of St Michaell the Archangell by equall portions &c.
Gervase Haywood

Dame Anne her jointure. 1650.
Asshover. £250 p. ann.

engrossment.title: The engrossment of the release of Asshover

parts.text: Three skins of parchment stitched at the head, unsealed, written throughout in one engrossing hand: Daniel Wragg's. The first skin begins:
This Indenture

made the nine and twentieth day of September in the twelfth yeare of the reigne of our Soveraigne Lord Charles the Second, by the grace of God of England, Scotland, France and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith &c., Betweene Sir Gervase Haywood of Wynstanton in the County of Derby, Baronet, of the one part, and Thomas Pargeter, Citizen and Alderman of London, of the other part &c.
The second skin, held to the window. At the fourteenth line:

…hath granted, bargained, sold, released and confirmed unto the said Thomas Pargeter (in his actuall possession now being by vertue of a bargaine and sale for one whole yeare &c.) All that the Mannor or Lordshipp of Asshover in the said County of Derby, with all its rights, members and appurtenances, and all messuages, lands, tenements, meadowes, pastures, woods and commons thereunto belonging,
together with all mines, mineralls and quarries
in and under the same, To have and to hold the said Mannor and premisses unto the said Thomas Pargeter, his heires and assignes for ever &c.
Below the third skin the seal tags hang empty.

Mr Cressy,

I have yours of the 15th, with the draught. The Asshover ore assayes better than we hoped, & my man is confident of the veine. See the mines pass with the land, and spare no reasonable cost.

Your loving friend,
Tho. Pargeter

_papers_schema.canon: Every text holds its clue's fact (design/case/case-1660.json clues) and nothing past it. Invented and harmless: the settlement's day (6 May 1650), the wording of the deeds, the corrections in the draft, the address and the bond sentence in Pargeter's letter (canon: the sale clears the £2,000 bond). Dates: Charles II's twelfth regnal year runs 30 Jan 1660 to 29 Jan 1661; James I's tenth year (24 Mar 1612 to 23 Mar 1613) holds the whole legal year 1612, which began on Lady Day.
